prompt: Name the cell at the surface of a root that is specialised for absorbing water, and name the process by which water enters it.
answer: The root hair cell; water enters by osmosis.
explanation: Osmosis moves water from where it is more dilute to where it is more concentrated, across a partially permeable membrane. Soil water is more dilute than the cell sap inside the root hair, so water moves inward without the plant spending any energy on it.

prompt: Name the type of joint found at the shoulder, the type found at the elbow, and state which of the two allows movement in more directions.
answer: A ball-and-socket joint at the shoulder; a hinge joint at the elbow. The ball-and-socket allows movement in more directions.
explanation: The shape of the bone ends sets the range: a rounded head sitting in a cup can swing and rotate in every direction, while a hinge is shaped to move in one plane only. The wider range is paid for in stability, which is why shoulders dislocate far more often than elbows.

prompt: State what is meant by an antagonistic muscle pair, and name the pair that raises and lowers the human forearm.
answer: Two muscles that work against each other, one contracting while the other relaxes, to move a bone in opposite directions. The biceps and the triceps.
explanation: A muscle can only pull, never push, so a bone can be moved back only by a second muscle on the other side of the joint. The biceps contracts to bend the elbow and the triceps contracts to straighten it, and both cannot contract fully at the same time.

prompt: State TWO structural features of a vein, and state the function of veins.
answer: A thin muscular wall, a wide lumen, and valves along its length (any two). Veins carry blood back toward the heart.
explanation: Blood in a vein is at low pressure, having already passed through the capillary beds, so a thick wall is unnecessary and a wide lumen reduces resistance. The valves matter because low pressure alone cannot push blood uphill from the legs; they stop it falling back between squeezes of the surrounding muscles.

prompt: Name the blood vessel that carries blood from the left ventricle to the body, and the vessel that carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
answer: The aorta carries blood from the left ventricle to the body; the pulmonary artery carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
explanation: Both are arteries, because both carry blood away from the heart — which is the definition, regardless of what the blood contains. The pulmonary artery is the one artery in the body carrying deoxygenated blood, and the pulmonary vein the one vein carrying oxygenated blood.

prompt: State what is meant by a trophic level, and state which trophic level a producer occupies.
answer: A feeding level in a food chain — the position an organism occupies according to how many steps it is from the producer. A producer occupies the first trophic level.
explanation: Trophic level describes a position rather than a species, which is why an omnivore can occupy two levels at once in the same ecosystem. Counting levels from the producer is what makes the 10% rule and the shape of an energy pyramid meaningful.

prompt: Name the transport tissue that lies just inside the bark of a tree trunk, and name the meristem that lies between the bark and the wood.
answer: Phloem lies just inside the bark; the cambium (vascular cambium) lies between the bark and the wood.
explanation: This arrangement explains why a complete ring cut through the bark is fatal. It removes the phloem all the way round, so no food can reach the roots, while the xylem deeper in the trunk continues to carry water up — the leaves go on working for months while the roots starve.

prompt: State THREE structural adaptations of a xerophyte that reduce water loss.
answer: Any three of: a thick waxy cuticle; sunken stomata; fewer stomata, mostly on the lower surface; rolled leaves; leaves reduced to spines; hairs on the leaf surface; a fleshy water-storing stem.
explanation: Most of these work the same way — by trapping a layer of humid air next to the stomata, so that the gradient driving evaporation is smaller. The plant is not sealing itself shut, because it must still admit carbon dioxide; it is slowing the loss that admitting it costs.

prompt: Name the TWO circuits of a mammal's double circulation, and state which one carries blood to the lungs.
answer: The pulmonary circulation and the systemic circulation. The pulmonary circulation carries blood to the lungs.
explanation: Blood passes through the heart twice in one complete journey, which is what double circulation means. Keeping the circuits separate lets the systemic side be pumped at a much higher pressure than the delicate lung capillaries could withstand, so the body is supplied quickly without damaging the lungs.

prompt: Name the FOUR components of human blood.
answer: Plasma, red blood cells (erythrocytes), white blood cells (leucocytes) and platelets (thrombocytes).
explanation: Plasma is about 55% of the volume and is mostly water, carrying dissolved food, hormones, urea, salts and carbon dioxide. The three cellular components each do one job: red cells transport oxygen, white cells defend against infection, and platelets clot the blood at a wound.

prompt: Name TWO abiotic factors and TWO biotic factors in an ecosystem.
answer: Abiotic: temperature, light, water, soil type, pH, wind, humidity. Biotic: predation, competition, disease, parasitism, the availability of food organisms.
explanation: Abiotic factors are the non-living conditions and biotic factors are the effects of other living things. The distinction matters ecologically because abiotic factors act on a population regardless of its density, while most biotic factors bite harder as a population becomes more crowded.

prompt: Name TWO processes that release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, and name the process that removes it.
answer: Released by: respiration, combustion (burning) of fuels, decomposition, volcanic activity (any two). Removed by photosynthesis.
explanation: For most of the Earth's history these were roughly in balance, which is what kept the atmospheric concentration steady. Burning fossil fuels breaks the balance by releasing carbon that was locked away for hundreds of millions of years, faster than photosynthesis can take it back.

prompt: State what is meant by wilting, and name the cells that close a stoma.
answer: Wilting is the drooping of a plant's leaves and soft stems when its cells lose turgor through water loss. Stomata are closed by the guard cells.
explanation: Guard cells close a stoma by losing water and becoming flaccid, so the pore between them shuts. Wilting is therefore not simply damage — a wilted plant has closed its stomata and reduced the surface it presents to the air, which slows further loss while the roots catch up.

prompt: State TWO features of a root hair cell that increase the rate at which it absorbs water.
answer: Any two of: a long thin extension giving a very large surface area; a thin cell wall and membrane giving a short diffusion distance; a large permanent vacuole holding concentrated cell sap; no chloroplasts, and many mitochondria to supply ATP for active transport of minerals.
explanation: The extension is the key one, because it multiplies the surface in contact with soil water enormously for very little extra material. Root hairs are short-lived and constantly replaced just behind the growing tip, which is why transplanting a seedling roughly damages so much of its absorbing surface.

prompt: Name THREE functions of the human skeleton.
answer: Any three of: support of the body; protection of organs; movement, by providing attachment for muscles; production of blood cells in the red bone marrow; storage of minerals such as calcium and phosphorus.
explanation: The last two are easily forgotten because they are not mechanical. Bone is an active tissue with its own blood supply, continually being broken down and rebuilt, and it acts as the body's calcium reserve — which is why a diet short of calcium weakens the skeleton over time.

prompt: Name the bones that make up the rib cage, and state ONE function of the rib cage.
answer: The ribs, the sternum (breastbone) and the thoracic vertebrae. It protects the heart and lungs, and it moves during breathing to change the volume of the thoracic cavity.
explanation: The rib cage has to do two things that pull against each other: shield the organs inside and still move freely twelve or more times a minute. Costal cartilage at the front is what makes both possible, giving the join to the sternum enough flexibility to allow the ribs to swing.

prompt: State the function of white blood cells and the function of platelets.
answer: White blood cells defend the body against infection, by engulfing pathogens or producing antibodies. Platelets bring about the clotting of blood at a wound.
explanation: Both are defences, against different threats. White cells deal with what gets in, and platelets deal with the opening it got in through — a clot seals the wound, stops further blood loss, and closes the entry point to any further pathogens.

prompt: State approximately what percentage of the energy at one trophic level is passed on to the next, and state what happens to the rest.
answer: About 10%. The remaining 90% is lost as heat from respiration, in undigested material (faeces), in excretion, and in parts not eaten.
explanation: This loss at every step is why food chains rarely exceed four or five links — after four transfers there is too little energy left to support another level. It is also why a pyramid of energy is always upright, however odd a pyramid of numbers for the same chain may look.
